<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: \26\George Mason University, J. McGinn, No. 6 Building Resilience: Mobilizing the Defense Industrial Base in an Era of Great-Power Competition (Sep. 28, 2020).
\27\E.O. 13806, Assessing and Strengthening the Manufacturing and Defense Industrial Base and Supply Chain Resiliency of the United States (Jul. 26, 2017); E.O. 14017, America's Supply Chains (Feb. 24, 2021).
\28\White House, Memorandum on the Presidential Waiver of Statutory Requirements Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (Oct. 3, 2022).
\29\White House, FACT SHEET: President Biden Takes Bold Executive Action to Spur Domestic Clean Energy Manufacturing (Jun. 6, 2022).
\30\White House, Additional Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions (Mar. 14, 2025).
Analysis: H.R. 7688 is a strongly bipartisan bill that expands oversight, improves function, limits the president's power where it matters, and strengthens the law. Generally, the bill would narrow the use of Title I authorities to a declared national emergency, a Stafford Act natural disaster, or a public health emergency. It would allow the President to delegate certain responsibilities to designated agencies, and it would affirmatively anchor the DPA Fund in the Department of the Treasury. Further, civil penalties would rise from $10,000 to $100,000, while potential criminal penalties would be removed.
The bill would increase the DPA Fund cap from $750 million to $2 billion, expanding potential application of the law's authorities. It would also raise the threshold at which Congressional notice is required from $50 million to $100 million. At the same time, however, the bill would require significantly more detailed planning for the use of those funds: After restructuring the DPAC, the bill would mandate a DPA Strategy to identify potential threats, live ``table-top'' exercises to devise mobilization plans to address those threats (reflecting a bill from Rep. Green, H.R. 8071, the ``Strengthening and Improving Mobilization Act of 2026''), and a supply-chain strategy covering medical materials, critical minerals, and naval shipbuilding capacity. The bill would also require an analysis of foreign adversary control risks and another, from Rep. Fields' H.R. 8136, the ``DPA Advanced Procurement Act of 2026,'' on long-lead items and stockpiling. Reporting to Congress (in a far more extensive manner than is currently required) would be required for all activities.
H.R. 7688 addresses several industrial areas critical to the national defense. For critical minerals, there would be a targeted initiative to speed planning, procurement, and infrastructure permitting. For emerging technologies, reflecting a bill from Rep. Lynch, H.R. 8053, the ``DPA Emerging Technologies Act,'' there would be established a subcommittee of the DPAC that would examine how artificial intelligence and robotics, biotechnology, cryptography and quantum computing, materials science, semiconductors, space might be leveraged for the national defense within and across agencies and sectors. This subcommittee would study the potential for a strategic biomaterials reserve, as recommended by members of the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology. The DPAC would be permitted to establish additional subcommittees. It would also require outreach and support to firms that offer goods and services necessary to the national defense, consistent with a bill from Rep. Beatty, H.R. 8038, the ``DPA Private-Sector Outreach Act of 2026.''
To address critical skills gaps, the bill reflects legislation from Rep. Casten, H.R. 8133, the ``DPA Workforce and Skilled Labor Needs Act of 2026,'' affirming that DPA funds could be used to support recruitment, training, placement, or retention of defense-critical workers and apprenticeships. Agencies would be required to report to Congress on steps needed to bolster the workforce to support the national defense. The bill would also adopt language from Rep. Gottheimer's H.R. 8138, the ``DPA Specialized Staffing Act,'' that would grant special hiring authority for subject matter experts to assist agencies with specialized financing focus and decisions.
Reflecting concern about trends of the last 13 months, the bill would cap future DPA-funded equity investments to 15% and would require a determination that private capital is unavailable. The bill would also require timely liquidation of such equity, when commercially feasible. Further, the bill would require the agencies using DPA authorities to take equity shares to provide Congress with the terms of the agreements-- information that has not been shared for most of the transactions where President Trump has used taxpayer dollars for private-sector equity ownership.
Addressing ethics issues, the bill includes Ranking Member Waters' H.R. 8030, the ``DPA Transparency Act of 2026,'' that would enact conflicts-of-interest language that would cover the President, Vice President, certain cabinet officials, or their immediate family members, including sons- and daughters-in-law. If those individuals hold 20% or more ownership in an entity, DPA assistance would be barred to those entities. In cases where there are two or more covered individuals that have an interest in an entity, those interests are aggregated to determine if they meet the cap. The bill would also require DPA agencies to institute fraud risk management standards.
The bill also incorporates components of Rep. Himes' H.R. 3542, the ``CLEAR (Committee Leadership and Enhanced Accountability for Resilience) Defense Production Act of 2025,'' which would make improvements to DPAC management and function, are also included, as are elements to support future health emergencies, drawn from a bill from Rep. Vargas.
While the bill is a product of collaboration between Chairman Hill and Ranking Member Waters, two amendments that would have improved the bill were offered by the Democratic caucus and denied by the majority. Both represent critical, timely issues raised in the headlines during the week prior the markup.
The first amendment, offered by Ranking Member Waters, would have established a rule of construction to prevent DPA authorities from being used in presidentially declared emergencies related to domestic federal elections. The Washington Post\31\ and other media\32\ reported that the Trump Administration has been circulating a 17-page draft executive order that claims that China interfered in the 2020 election. In that draft order, Trump refers to the Defense Production Act authorities three times, attempting to build the case for being able to suggest voting machines are invalid and must be replaced by his own approved methods of vote casting and counting. The amendment was rejected on party lines.
\31\Washington Post, A. Arnsdorf, Trump, seeking executive power over elections, is urged to declare emergency (Feb. 26, 2026).
\32\Democracy Docket, M. Cohen, J. Saksa, Read a draft of the emergency executive order for Trump to take control of elections (Feb. 27, 2026).
The second amendment was offered by Rep. Liccardo, reflecting the Trump Administration's highly unusual actions towards Anthropic. His amendment aimed to stop the Department of Defense from using DPA to retaliate against developers for instituting safeguards on high-risk technologies. Noting the Trump Administration's ire at Anthropic for the AI company's effort to set guardrails that would prevent its products and services from being used for mass surveillance of U.S. citizens or autonomous weapons, the amendment proposed to prevent such abuses. It was rejected on party lines.
We support the underlying bill will continue to work on these amendments and to improve the bill as it moves to the floor.
